query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: The thin-wall as-deposited samples of Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr alloy with the size of 50 mm (length) × 12 mm (height) × 3 mm (width) were prepared with a self-assembling laser melting deposition (LMD) process system, which consisted of a 3 kW semiconductor laser with the wavelength of 900–1070 nm, a coaxial powder feeding nozzle, a DPSF-2 powder feeder with two hoppers, a computer numerical control (CNC) platform and a glove box filled with argon. Figure 3a displays the schematic diagram of the LMD process and the deposition path. The LMD process was conducted using laser power of 600 W, 800 W, 1000 W, 1200 W and 1400 W, scanning rate of 4 mm/s, powder feeding rate of 8 g/min and height increment of 0.5 mm of each layer. As-deposited samples prepared with five different process parameters is shown in Figure 3b and all these samples were measured and evaluated using a Vickers hardness tester. The as-deposited alloy sample with better hardness was selected for tensile mechanical test.

The elemental metal powders of the four different tungsten mole alloys were accurately measured by the electronic, analytical balance before the experiment. Powders were mixed for 4 h via SYH three-dimensional motion mixer series to ensure that they were mixed evenly. Then, the mixed powders were put into a vacuum oven at 120 °C to dry for 8 h in order to remove moisture and enhance the liquidity of the powder. The atmosphere chamber was filled with Argon gas to ensure that the oxygen content of the environment was lower than 80 ppm for the purpose of protecting the powders from being oxidized during the forming process. The LCD processing parameters in the experiments after optimizing were 565 W laser power, 8 mm/s scanning speed, 0.08 mm thickness of the deposited layer, and 600 °C induction heating temperature. The substrates and the formed area were heated during the forming process to reduce the internal stress. The crystal structures of the four different tungsten mole alloys were identified on the cross-section surfaces, using Bruker D8 Advanced A25 X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker AXS GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany) equipment. Room temperature tensile properties were evaluated using a CMT4105 universal electronic tensile testing machine at the strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1. Dog bone–shaped tensile samples with a section of 1.3 mm by 5 mm and a gauge length of 20 mm were cut by an electrical discharging machine.
All tests were examined at the crosshead speed of 0.36 mm/min, which imposed the strain rate of 10−3 s−1 on the samples.

In the present study, high-purity raw materials (i.e., Al [99.99%], Ti [99.99%], Nb [99.99%], Cr [99.99%], V [99.9%], and Zr [99.99%]) were prepared to form Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs. Master alloys were fabricated by performing arc-melting in an argon atmosphere with a Ti-getter to prevent oxidation, and each master alloy was remelted four times to ensure alloy homogeneity. The master alloys were further made into ingots by performing tilt casting in an argon atmosphere. The dimension of each fabricated ingot was 40 mm (length) × 20 mm (width) × 10 mm (thickness). In addition, the ingots were homogenized at 1000 °C for 2 h in a high vacuum atmosphere (<10−5 torr) and then water quenched for subsequent thermomechanical treatment. To detect phase transformation within the working temperature range (25–1100 °C), a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC; STA 449 F3 Jupiter, Netzsch, Bavaria, Germany) was used at a heating rate of 10 K/min in an argon atmosphere.

decision.rationale: The intervention of laser surface melting (direction A) addresses the limitation of inadequate oxygen resistance in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr by creating a dense, oxide-free surface layer. The critic's review suggests that this intervention is viable with changes, and the main risk is that the laser surface melting process may alter the underlying microstructure and affect the mechanical properties of the alloy. To mitigate this risk, further investigation into the effects of laser surface melting on the mechanical properties of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is necessary. The evidence from records PMC10254787, PMC9506522, PMC6385082, PMC7514121, and PMC7299626 supports the effectiveness of laser surface melting in improving surface properties, but direct evidence for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is limited.
